summary: Introduces a generic mechanism in the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol to group Label Switched Paths. Groups can express associations between sets of paths or between paths and sets of attributes, and apply to stateful PCE in active and passive modes and to stateless PCE.

eli5.summary: This lets a path planner put routes into labeled groups, like sorting toys into boxes, so it can treat related ones together.

questions: what is the pcep association object
what is an lsp association group
what is an operator-configured association range
subtitle: A generic PCEP object for putting Label Switched Paths into named groups so related paths can share policy and behavior.

tldr.problem: Several LSPs often need to share information, such as a working and a protection path, a path before and after reoptimization, or a set of diverse paths, and each use case would otherwise need its own mechanism.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8697 defines one ASSOCIATION object, identified by Association Type, Association ID and Association Source, plus two OPEN-object TLVs to advertise supported types and the range of IDs reserved for operator-configured groups.
tldr.outcome: Specific Association Types are left to future documents. This RFC supplies the common container and its rules. It has since been updated by RFC 9756.

today: RFC 8697 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9756. It is not obsoleted, so it remains the base definition of PCEP association groups together with that update.

sections.title: Why Group LSPs
sections.content:
A stateful PCE can update existing LSPs and create new ones. Often several LSPs must share information. The RFC gives examples: PCE-controlled make-before-break needs an association between the original and reoptimized path, end-to-end protection needs one between working and protection LSPs, and diverse paths can use a group of LSPs. A group can also simply apply a common set of configuration parameters or behaviors.

A stateless PCE can benefit too: a path computation request can be tied to an association group so a common policy applies to it. Some associations are created dynamically, such as working and protection LSPs of a tunnel. Others are created by the operator, such as a policy-based group that an LSP can join. Rather than build a mechanism per use case, the RFC defines one generic mechanism.

It is not the same thing as the SVEC object of RFC 5440, which synchronizes a set of requests. The motivations differ, though some use cases overlap, and any new Association Type should explain its relationship to SVEC.
sections.eli5: Some routes belong together, like a main road and its backup. Putting them in the same labeled box lets the planner remember that and give the box a rule.

sections.title: How Association Groups Work
sections.content:
An LSP joins a group by being added to a common association group. Groups can span LSPs from the same headend or different headends. A group is either dynamic, created and numbered by a PCEP speaker, or operator-configured, where the operator sets the Association ID, Association Type and Association Source by hand. An LSP may join several groups, of the same type or different types. Each Association Type has its own ID space.

The group is a property of the LSP and lives in the LSP state database. A dynamic association exists as long as the LSP state exists, and a group with no LSPs is considered empty and deleted. The Association Source is normally the local PCEP speaker address, unless local policy says otherwise. For configured groups it could be a PCEP speaker, a network management system or any other valid IP address.

What each Association Type means is outside this document. This RFC only creates the grouping container and the IANA registry for types.
sections.eli5: Each box has a name made from its kind, its number and who made it. A toy can sit in more than one box, and an empty box is thrown away.

sections.title: Advertising Association Types and Ranges
sections.content:
Two optional TLVs go in the OPEN object during session setup. The ASSOC-Type-List TLV (type 35) lists, as 2-byte code points, the Association Types the sender supports. It MUST NOT appear more than once, or the session MUST be rejected with Error-Type 1 and Error-value 1. A peer that does not recognize it ignores it. If an Association Type says its advertisement is mandatory, a missing entry means the type is not supported. The absence of the whole TLV only means there is no information.

The OP-CONF-ASSOC-RANGE TLV (type 29) tells the peer which Association IDs are reserved for operator-configured groups, so that dynamic groups never clash with them. Each entry has a Reserved field, an Assoc-Type, a Start-Assoc-ID and a Range, each 2 bytes. Start-Assoc-ID of 0 or 0xffff is invalid. Range must be greater than 0 and Start-Assoc-ID plus Range must not pass 0xffff. Bad values, or overlapping ranges for one type, cause the session to be rejected with Error-Type 1 and Error-value 1. Dynamic associations MUST NOT use IDs from this range.
sections.eli5: Before they start, the two planners swap lists of the kinds of boxes they understand, and tell each other which box numbers are kept for hand-made boxes.

sections.title: The ASSOCIATION Object
sections.content:
The ASSOCIATION object has Object-Class 40. Object-Type 1 carries an IPv4 Association Source and Object-Type 2 carries an IPv6 one. After a Reserved field and a Flags field come the Association Type and the Association ID, then the source address and optional TLVs.

The only flag defined is R (Removal). When set in a PCRpt or PCUpd, it asks to remove the LSP from the group. When unset, the LSP is added or kept. The Association ID values 0 and 0xffff are reserved, and 0xffff means all groups. Combined with R it removes the LSP from all associations in the scope of that type and source.

The combination of Association Type, Association ID and Association Source uniquely identifies a group. The optional Global Association Source TLV (type 30) and Extended Association ID TLV (type 31), taken from RFC 6780, are part of that identity when present. The format is aligned with the RSVP ASSOCIATION object.
sections.eli5: The label on a box says what kind it is, its number, who made it, and has a tick box that means take this toy out.

sections.title: Using the Object in PCEP Messages
sections.content:
In stateful operation the object MAY appear in PCUpd, PCRpt and PCInitiate messages, in a list. A PCRpt reports group membership to a stateful PCE. The first report of an LSP MUST include all its groups, and later reports SHOULD include only changed or removed ones. During state synchronization, an LSP's associations MUST be included. A delegated LSP can be put into new or existing groups by the PCE using a PCUpd, and a PCInitiate MUST list all the groups of the new LSP.

For a passive PCE, stateful or stateless, the object is optional in a PCReq and MAY appear in a PCRep carrying a NO-PATH object, where it names the group that caused the failure. In a PCReq, the group should already be known, either configured or learned earlier, and the R flag MUST be 0.

When a PCEP session ends, dynamic associations are cleared along with the LSP state, following the State Timeout Interval rules of RFC 8231. If an LSP is delegated to another PCE after a failure, the associations stay unless the new PCE changes them. When a delegation is revoked, the PCC MAY clear the PCE's associations, and SHOULD do so make-before-break.
sections.eli5: Planners can say, this route goes in that box, or take it out. If they stop talking, the boxes they made are tidied away with their routes.

sections.title: Association Errors
sections.content:
Problems are reported with a PCErr of Error-Type 26 (Association Error). A speaker that understands the object but not the Association Type MUST answer with value 1. Too many LSPs in a group gives value 2, and too many groups gives value 3. Both limits MAY be set by the operator or local policy. A PCReq that names an unknown association, or a removal of an unknown one, gives value 4. Mismatched information gives value 5 for operator-configured groups and value 6 for others. A failure to join a group gives value 7, and an ID outside the operator-configured range gives value 8.

A speaker that does not recognize the object at all answers with the Unknown Object error of RFC 5440. Invalid association parameters make the object malformed.
sections.eli5: If a planner cannot do what the label asks, it replies with a numbered complaint, such as I do not know that kind of box, that box is full, or there is no such box.

sections.title: Security and Manageability
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 8231 and RFC 5440 apply. Associations could be spoofed and used as an attack vector. An attacker could create too many to load the peer, which then replies with a PCErr, or create bogus ones to disturb LSP operations. Groups could also let an eavesdropper see the relationship between LSPs. The RFC therefore RECOMMENDS securing the PCEP session with TLS. It also advises using indirect values in the object to hide sensitive business relationships.

For manageability, a PCE or PCC implementation MUST allow operator-configured associations and SHOULD allow setting the operator-configured range. It SHOULD let the operator view configured and dynamic associations. The RFC notes no new liveness, verification or other-protocol requirements.
sections.eli5: Someone sneaky could make up fake boxes or peek at which routes belong together, so the planners should talk over a locked connection.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to 0 and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Holds the R (Removal) bit; unassigned flags are set to 0.

fields.name: Association Type
fields.desc: Kind of association, from the IANA registry.

fields.name: Association ID
fields.desc: Identifies the group; 0 and 0xffff are reserved.

items.label: Association Type is not supported
items.desc: The object is understood but the type is not.

items.label: Too many LSPs in the association group
items.desc: The group is over the allowed size.

items.label: Too many association groups
items.desc: The speaker cannot handle a new association.

items.label: Association unknown
items.desc: The named group is not known.

items.label: Operator-configured association information mismatch
items.desc: Peer information differs from local configuration.

items.label: Association information mismatch
items.desc: Information differs from what the same peer sent before.

items.label: Cannot join the association group
items.desc: The LSP could not be added for some reason.

items.label: Association ID not in range
items.desc: The ID is outside the operator-configured range.
